prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its translation into long-acting incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part B014 prize for Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. After reading all six first-round files, the scientific case is the same one I made before. The mechanism is stable and replicated. Holst established the human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action. Drucker defined the proglucagon-derived peptides and their intestinotropic and metabolic biology. Knudsen solved the half-life problem through acylation and albumin binding, which produced liraglutide and semaglutide. Large independent outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease confirm the effect, so I see no maturity objection. The three contributions are distinct and each was decisive for the next step. The discovery changed a field because the hormone became a medicine, so the citation should name both. The round-1 files show that the committee's remaining question is a narrow one about the third name and the scope of the citation. It is not a question about whether the science is ready.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my configuration is the one Marie makes. A trio of Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is a hybrid, with two physiologists and one drug designer, and it leaves out Mojsov, whose identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide is a real contribution. The three-person cap forces this exclusion, and Habener, who is outside the supplied credit list, is part of the same priority record. Naming an industrial contribution beside academic discoverers can be read as rewarding development over discovery. Long-term safety of the incretin class is still accumulating, and I cannot verify the latest data from the supplied materials. I also hold the view that the cap should not be allowed to hide the attribution question, so I treat the exclusion as a real cost and not as a technicality.

responses.point: Marie proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with a discovery-side citation. She argues this is the cleaner and more consistent reading of the Nobel tradition, and she says the Knudsen version would turn the prize into a hybrid, though she would not block it.
responses.response: This is the strongest alternative to my position and I have weighed it again. The discovery trio is internally consistent, and it keeps the committee from deciding on industrial drug design. My reasons for staying with Knudsen are these. First, the shortlisted achievement is framed as GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin therapies, so the development step is part of what we are judging. Second, the citation then rests on a step whose scientific content is clear, which is the pharmacokinetic design that extended the half-life from minutes to days, and that was not routine optimisation. Third, Mojsov's priority claim is real but is the least settled part of the record. I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence, and I would not build a citation on the point I am least able to verify. I disagree with your wording that this is merely a hybrid. Past prizes have recognised a discovery together with the step that realised it as a therapeutic principle. I would still accept a clearly worded discovery-only citation if the committee records that as a deliberate choice about scope.

responses.point: Per, as chair, names Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and says he would accept Mojsov in place of Knudsen if the committee prefers a discovery-only citation, provided the reasoning is stated explicitly. He also says the contested priority edge is not a contested core.
responses.response: I correct my round-1 summary of your position. I described you as crediting Mojsov, but your file credits Knudsen, and the chair's summary has it right. On substance, we agree. I want to test your last point rather than only repeat it. Holst and Drucker are secure under any reading, and I still think so. But the fourth name changes what the citation can say, so a contested edge is not irrelevant to the wording. If the committee goes with Knudsen, the record should say plainly that Mojsov's identification of the active peptide and Habener's early proglucagon work were considered and that the cap forced the exclusion. That is a more honest account than a citation that implies no such claim exists. I would support that statement in the committee's record.

responses.point: Rickard prefers the same trio but is concerned that attribution not be settled by default, familiarity, or the unanimity of the opening ballots. He also would not combine B014 with CAR-T as a two-part prize unless the committee accepts the credit gap.
responses.response: I share both concerns. On unanimity, our six first-place votes should not matter in the final discussion, and I have tried to make the case again from the science alone. On pairing, I considered a second part with B006. A June and Sadelain pair would be the most defensible CAR-T credit, but with the three-person cap, adding them to a B014 trio would force one of the GLP-1 names out or leave the CAR-T part unfairly narrow, with Rosenberg and Eshhar both outside it. That makes a two-part configuration worse on attribution than a single prize. B014 does not need a second part to be complete, so I keep it as a single-part prize and I hold B006 as my strongest alternative if the committee decides the GLP-1 credit cannot be defended.

responses.point: Abdel keeps Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and asks the committee to say whether a single GLP-1 prize is better than pairing it with a second achievement such as CAR-T. He also notes that long-term safety data on incretin therapies could affect the citation.
responses.response: On pairing, I answer no, for the reason I give to Rickard: the cap forces cuts that make both parts weaker. On safety, I would not treat the open long-term questions as a reason to delay. The efficacy and cardiovascular and renal outcome data are large and independent, and what remains is the safety profile of an established class. I would handle this in the citation by confining the claim to the established indications, type 2 diabetes and obesity, and not by extending it to benefits that are still being studied. I also noted your point that optogenetics is among your top four. I agree its science is mature, but I do not see an allocation among six names that holds up, so I keep it only as an alternative and not as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will record a discovery-plus-translation citation (Drucker, Holst, Knudsen) or a discovery-only citation (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov), and whether the supplied evidence is enough to justify excluding Mojsov, or Knudsen, with stated reasons.
Whether Mojsov's and Habener's priority on early GLP-1 and proglucagon work can be settled from the supplied materials. I do not believe it can.
Long-term safety and outcome data on the incretin class are still accumulating, and I cannot verify the latest trials from the supplied files.
If B014 is not awarded in this form, whether B006 can be given a fair credit with Eshhar outside the list, or B008 a defensible split among six names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any credited candidate on the shortlist. My documented ties are to nuclear-receptor research with Ronald Evans, collaboration with Johan Ericson, and co-authorship with Per Svenningsson (about twenty works) and Abdel El-Manira (one 2009 paper). None concerns GLP-1, CAR-T, optogenetics or any other shortlisted ballot. I do not infer further ties from shared institutions or topics, and I do not request recusal.
